newsitem.title: NIGERIA: FEATURE - Nigerian ruler digs in three years after coup.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Nigerian ruler digs in three years after coup.

text.p: A rare public appearance by Nigerian military ruler Sani Abacha recently provided clear evidence that the dapper infantry general is well entrenched in power three years after his bloodless coup.
The occasion was Nigeria's 36th anniversary of independence, when Abacha showed up on the parade ground in the capital Abuja for a celebration highlighted by thunderous chanting and dancing.
"Neither his friends nor his enemies would have given him much chance in November 1993 when he staged his coup," said Dare Babarinsa, executive editor of the opposition Tell magazine.
"Now he is still there and may still be there past the year 2000," he wrote in his political column.
Speculation is rife that Abacha might follow the example of other coup leaders in West Africa and contest a presidential poll set for 1998 to transform himself into an elected leader.
"The armed forces have no intention to remain in power beyond 1998," Abacha said in a message to an army conference in the northern city of Sokoto on November 4.

A few days later his information minister, Walter Ofonagoro, said at a forum at the Dan Fodio University in Sokoto that "the head of state is not a civilian and has stated categorically that he will not contest the 1998 presidential election".
But such clarifications have failed to extinguish the feeling among Abacha's critics that he plans to hang on to power.
"The regime has its own agenda of self-perpetuation," says Sylvester Odion-Akhaine, general secretary of the anti-government Campaign for Democracy pressure group.
His counterpart at the Committee for the Defence of Human Rights, Shina Loremikan, said: "By design, acts and action, the Abacha junta has no intention to leave in 1998."
"Their doubts may persist until Abacha actually hands over," wrote political correspondent Ade Olorunfewa in Tell magazine.

Abacha took power on November 17, 1993, when Africa's most populous and multi-ethnic nation of more than 100 million was on the verge of breaking up over the annulment of a presidential election won by millionaire businessman Moshood Abiola.

While the issue of the annulled vote has not been resolved, Abacha last year launched an elaborate programme he said would lead to full democracy from October 1, 1998, and politicians have already joined the quest for power.
Abiola and several of his supporters are either in detention or exile, leaving Abacha with scant opposition at home.
The situation is a far cry from 1994 when Abiola declared himself president and was thrown into jail.
Riots and strikes by the powerful oil unions gripped the nation for months until Abacha finally acted by sacking and detaining the union leaders.

His handling of that crisis gave the first hint that behind his trademark dark glasses lay an iron will that was to manifest itself soon after with radical economic reforms, including a four-fold increase in pump prices of fuel.
"No head of state in this country has ever increased the price of fuel without people rioting," said Jimie Esho, a banker. "Abacha did it in 1994 and there were no riots."
He was to fight many battles, taking on those considered sacrosanct such as former head of state Olusegun Obasanjo and his deputy, who were jailed over an alleged coup plot.

But the diminutive general hit his lowest point on November 10, 1995, when nine minority rights activists including renowned author Ken Saro-Wiwa were hanged for the murder of four prominent chiefs from the volatile Ogoni oil-producing area.
Sanctions rained on Nigeria from far and near, it was expelled from the Commonwealth, and calls for an immediate return to democracy filled the air.
But a year later the intense pressure on Abacha seems to have dissipated.
Tough actions like jailing Nigerians found to have looted banks, macro-economic stability and reduced inflation have steadily brought him some good reviews, at least within Nigeria.
On the economic front he is contemplating privatisation of Nigeria's oil industry on a scale not seen in Africa and this is drawing the interest of multilateral lending agencies.
"The fact is that a lot of water has passed under the bridge in Nigeria since 1993," said an East African diplomat who has closely followed the Nigerian crisis.

"Human rights is still held very much against them but General Abacha succeeded in preventing a breakup of Nigeria. This is no small achievement considering what is happening elsewhere, like in Somalia and Rwanda," he added.

Abacha himself considers restoration of order his biggest achievement, although critics characterise this as "peace of the graveyard" and say nothing short of handing over to Abiola will resolve the crisis that led to the general's seizing power.
